issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: For a 45-year-old female auditor with combat trauma, 'Pregnancy/Birth Reminders' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other trigger items and downstream threat items center on hypervigilance, pursuit, and danger cues, whereas this item implies a reproductive/perinatal trigger theme that is not supported by the memory, threat, appraisal, or strategy content. It looks disconnected from the combat-based formulation rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: 'Restrict Eating' is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile. The dominant clinical pattern across triggers, threat, memory, and appraisals is fear-based hypervigilance and fragmented trauma memory, with maladaptive strategies of avoidance and rumination fitting that pattern. Restrictive eating instead suggests a separate control/body-management coping style that is not reflected elsewhere in the selected items, making it clinically hard to explain as part of the same combat-related PTSD profile.

vignette: Fatima, a 45-year-old divorced auditor of Middle Eastern descent, has been struggling with symptoms that have significantly impacted her daily life. The traumatic event she experienced occurred during her time in combat, where the relentless sounds of explosions and the smell of cologne from the surroundings became seared into her memory. Waking up from nightmares is a frequent occurrence for Fatima; these dreams often leave her disoriented and anxious, as if the chaos of the battlefield has followed her home. The remnants of these nightmares can linger throughout her day, making it difficult to focus on work or engage in social activities. One particular morning, after waking up from another nightmare, she found herself at work, overwhelmed by a strong cologne scent that reminded her of the soldiers' presence during combat. This olfactory trigger only intensified her feelings of vulnerability and fear. Fatima has come to believe that she should have protected others better during the event and that her inability to do so is tied directly to who she is as a person, which fuels her sense of failure. These negative appraisals have led her to constantly scan her environment for signs of threat, checking behind her frequently and always looking for escape routes. This hyper-vigilance has become a part of her daily routine, leaving little room for anything else. Her memories of the traumatic event are fragmented and incomplete. She cannot remember certain parts of what happened and feels like she only remembers pieces that do not fit together coherently. These gaps in memory have made it difficult for Fatima to fully process what she experienced. The lack of a cohesive narrative has led her to feel even more threatened, as the uncertainty around these missing pieces amplifies her anxiety. Fatima's hyper-vigilance and tendency to avoid open spaces often lead her to feel safe only in very limited locations. This restricted sense of safety exacerbates her negative appraisals, reinforcing her belief that she is a failure for not being able to protect others. Her constant checking and scanning also interfere with her ability to recall the event accurately; the more she focuses on threat, the less clear her memories become. One evening at work, Fatima was triggered by an explosion-like noise from the construction site across the street. This sound immediately transported her back to the battlefield, causing a wave of panic that made it impossible for her to continue working. Her mind raced with thoughts about how she should have done more and could not prevent the explosions from happening. The experience left her feeling physically and emotionally drained. Her counterfactual thinking—pondering how life would be different if the event had never occurred—has only deepened her sense of guilt and self-blame. These thoughts are particularly strong when she is in open or exposed spaces, where she feels more vulnerable. Fatima frequently checks behind her, convinced that danger lurks around every corner. The memories she does have come to her in disjointed fragments, further contributing to her feelings of threat and vulnerability. The lack of a coherent memory of the event has made it difficult for her to feel safe even when she is in familiar environments. Her body reacts as if it were still under attack, and she often finds herself reliving parts of the trauma. Fatima's life has become a series of avoidance behaviors and constant threat monitoring, making daily tasks increasingly challenging. The cumulative effect of these symptoms has strained her relationships with colleagues and friends. She no longer enjoys activities she once loved because they are too triggering or make her feel unsafe. What finally brought Fatima to seek help was the realization that her quality of life had deteriorated significantly. She was most afraid that she would never be able to fully process what happened and that these memories and fears would continue to control her life. Her hope is that through therapy, she can regain a sense of safety and find ways to manage her symptoms without letting them dictate every aspect of her daily routine.
